doc.title: Helen Oakley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Battle of Webb and Basie and Chick Webb's death
summary: The Basie battle exposed Webb's band, she lost interest, and Chick died soon after; she joined the OSS.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Oh good. Well I’ll just tell you end of that then, because the end was I knew I was fighting a losing battle. Well then I put on a battle of the bands between Chick and Basie. And you knew that there was only one answer there. Although Chick, he was a battler. And of course the sound of his drums, there was nothing like it. And that bass, that boom boom, that started up, the whole Savoy Ballroom used to, lift the floor. And so Chick held his own as far as the people were concerned. But there was really no comparison. And Billie wasn’t with the band, she’d left the band then, but anyway it was the Basie band. So after it was all over the Webb band called a meeting and said, “She set us up — she exposed us” you know, “she set us up.” And I didn’t care for the band anyway, and it wasn’t a wonderful band, and naturally they didn’t like me. And you know so, and Chick, by that time he was pretty ill, and he was frankly upset. And I said to him, you know, “Chick, if the office wants to fire me, let them. I’ve done my job, I’ve put you where you’re supposed to be and that’s what they hired me for.” And so that’s the end of that. And it really was, after that, I pretty well lost interest, and the thing was that he went to Baltimore and it broke my heart because he felt that he wanted me with him. And I should have been with him. And if he didn’t have a bad office I would have been with him whether, no matter, anything. And I used to worry and worry about him, and he was © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

progressively dying. And so in Baltimore he went and played another thing on board ship, and we were in white, Baltimore, and he was making signals to me to get over and to speak and everything and I didn’t. Because I didn’t want to get him in trouble either. I mean I could have also been in trouble, and I didn’t want to get him in trouble, so I didn’t. And it broke my heart because he was giving me that eye, that desperate eye, and I didn’t. And he went straight into Johns Hopkins and died five days later. And that was quite a heartbreaker. So after that I was approached by the OSS, and I thought — Rupert had died, that wonderful brother that Duke had loved too, and he died at Dieppe, you know the invasion of Dieppe. And I guess my heart had sort of gone out of things. So from my point of view, and probably yours, my career in jazz ended. I did do what I could for T-Bone, which was wonderful, but none of it compared with those.
